lines: That hinge has been off since the spring gales. I have the pin. I have the hammer.
Ask me about the hinge again next year and I will say this, in this tone, holding this cup.
My back. We are not going to discuss my back.
Somebody has been at the honey and I have narrowed it down to four people.
Two more baskets and then I sit down. I have said that twice already today.
The wind turns at about four. You can set the whole afternoon by it if you pay attention.
I want one day where nothing needs mending. One. I am not asking for a week.
The pump is fine. The pump has been fine for six years in the way that a thing about to break is fine.
Crates are packed and still stacked because the cart has a wheel off. One wheel. Six weeks.
That is my sister's shelf. Leave it as it is, please.
We are out of good nails, so today everything gets bad nails and a bit of hope.
Bread went wrong this morning. Same flour, same oven, same hands. No idea.
I count in springs, not years. Everybody here does. You get used to it in about a spring.
There is rot in the north corner post and I have been walking past it for a month.
The dog will not come in and will not settle out. So neither of us is sleeping.
If you are going up the path, take something with you. Nobody goes up the path empty-handed.
I have mended this net so many times that none of the original net is left in it.
It comes up about a hand's width a year. Slow enough to live with. That is the trap of it.
We moved up in my mother's time. Everybody has a moving-up in their family somewhere.
That was a street. Where the water is flat, there. That whole line was a street.
The salt reaches the wells a year or two before the water does. The well is the warning.
You do not notice it rising. You notice that a step you used to stand on is a step you swim to.
The maps are wrong and nobody redraws them because they would be wrong again before the ink dried.
Nobody says flood. We say the level. I did not notice we did that until somebody pointed it out.
We had a garden down there. Went salty. Now it is where the nets live, which is a demotion.
My grandfather learned to swim in a spot that is now forty strokes out from the shore.
The frogs move up a year before we do. It is not superstition, it is just that they are quicker.
You mark the door post every spring. The marks are a ladder and they only go one way.
Every family here has a house their grandparents built that you would need a boat to visit.
The old road runs down and into the water and keeps going, straight, for a good way.
We are not survivors of anything. We are the ones whose people stopped running. Different thing.
Do not build anything you love below the third post. That is not advice, that is the rule.
The bottom row goes first. The bottom row has always been going first. It just used to be further down.
There is a doorway out there that still swings when the current runs past it. I have seen it.
You can date a family here by which move they talk about as though it were recent.
The boat is named for my sister. She has been dead nineteen years and I say the name forty times a day.
There is a key on the nail by the door. The door it opens has been underwater since I was twenty.
I go down and touch the handle once a year. Then I come up and I do not talk about it.
My father cries when it rains hard and calls it the wind, and we all let him have the wind.
There is a bowl in this house with a blue bird on it that came out of somebody else's kitchen.
We use it. It is a good bowl. Not using it would not bring anybody back.
I can name every family from the low street in order. I do it when I cannot sleep. It works, oddly.
The stairs are still down there with the handrail on. You can hold it the whole way down.
Somebody cut two letters and a heart into a beam that has been underwater for thirty years.
There is a shelf in nearly every house here that belongs to somebody dead and stays empty.
We took a door off a drowned house and it is our table now. We eat off their front door.
The names last about two generations past the places. Then they go quiet as well.
A child's shoe came up in the shallows last spring. Small one. Nobody said anything for a while.
The garden gate down there is still shut. Somebody shut it on their way out, which is the part that gets me.
My brother saved a chair and lost a house in the same week and only ever mentions the chair.
I know exactly how deep it is at that corner because I have been down there in the dark.
We used to be a much bigger family. That is just a sentence. Everybody here has that sentence.
There is a bell in the old hall down there. People claim to hear it. Nobody hears it. We all understand why they say it.
The markers were flood markers, built by people who knew this was coming. That is what is said.
It is probably not true. It is also the reason two families here get out of bed. So.
The great wall was a dam and it failed, and the wall-walkers go looking for where it failed.
They will not find it. Not because it is hidden. Because there is nothing to find.
The ring of arches was a cistern, everyone says. We tell the children lions drank there.
Lions drank at the arches. Everyone knows that. Nobody has produced a lion.
The carved city was cut from the rock rather than built, so it is held to be older than the water.
Which would mean there was a before. That is what the argument is actually about, every time.
The calendar stone is supposed to say when it stops. It has been read a thousand ways and it says nothing.
Build like the mountain terraces and you live. That is the whole of upland thinking, in one sentence.
The tomb is for one person and it is the most beautiful thing there is. Nobody argues about the tomb.
That is what I find strange. Everything else is a fight, and the tomb just gets agreed with.
Nobody knows who built any of it. Everybody talks as though they do. Both of those are true.
Somebody chalked a marker line on the mill wall as though chalk would hold the water off.
I did not rub it out. Two families slept better that week. Work out the arithmetic on that.
The wall-walkers come through for salt. Always salt, always limping, always going straight back out.
There are seven things still standing and everything ordinary is underneath. People take that personally.
The wrong stories are holding things up. I would not want to be the one who pulled one out.
Somebody has to be able to read this book in fifty years. That is the whole reason for the copying.
I make the children copy pages until their hands cramp and I tell them exactly why, and they still hate it.
We are teaching everyone letters. Everyone. Including people who will never write a word.
The seeds go in wax at the back of the cold chamber. That set is not for us.
Do not ask me who it is for. I will answer and then neither of us will enjoy the rest of the day.
There is a shelf in the cave, planed smooth and pegged, empty, built to the size of books.
Whoever built that shelf measured a future and made furniture for it. I think about it often.
Half of us want to go higher and half of us want to stay and both halves are right, which is the problem.
The ones who went up send word back saying come up. Nobody who stayed has sent word saying stay.
Devi planted the whole row knowing she will be gone before it fruits.
She said somebody will come through hungry. That is the best argument I have heard in a year.
We cut names into stone now rather than write them on paper. That is a decision about how long.
I am training a replacement and I have not told her that is what I am doing.
The songs have all the place names in them on purpose, so the names outlive the places.
People keep asking when we are going up. I keep saying after the harvest. There have been four harvests.
There is a well going salty and a daughter up the path, and one of those will win eventually.
Nobody here is trying to fix it. We are trying to hand it over intact. Different job entirely.
The old ones apologise, at the end, every one of them. I have decided I am not going to do that.
You do the work. The work does not care whether it is going to be enough.
Bail in the morning, mend at noon, bail again before dark. That is the shape of it.
The boards are lethal when they have dried and got wet again. That is when people go in.
The tide table is not a suggestion. I will keep saying that until somebody drowns or listens.
Rope goes furry at the waterline. Furry means replace, not tighten. Tightening furry rope kills people.
Everything out here is tied to something else. Cut one line and you find out what else it was holding.
I have opinions about how much fish we eat and nobody has ever asked me for them.
The knot outlives the hand that ties it, which is a nice thing to say and also just true about rope.
Walk the outside boards leaning in. Do not look down, do not hurry, and do not carry two things.
Wind gets under the floor at the big tides and lifts the whole house about a finger's width.
I have put new legs under this house twice and both times they went in longer. That is the whole history of the place.
You can date a house by counting the rungs added to its ladder. Ours has eleven.
There were four rows out past this one. Now there is us, and then there is the water.
At the big tides the sea comes over the boards and we all lift our feet and keep talking.
The uplanders call us stubborn. We call them cowards. Neither side entirely means it.
You can see roofs under us on a still day. You stop finding that strange after about a year.
We are the last row. The last row has always been somebody. It used to be somebody further out.
Nobody out here says flood. We say the level, or this year, or the tides.
Anzu ties on to a chimney when the wind turns. It was her aunt's chimney, when it had a house under it.
Once a year the tide drops far enough to show the top of the schoolyard fence, and then it covers it again.
The children dare each other to touch it. I did the same at their age. It is only a railing.
I was born in a room that is directly under where we are standing. My mother pointed it out once.
The old well is down there, full of sea water. We call that a joke. It is not one.
Every year on her day somebody swims down and leaves something on the ledge, and every year the sea takes it back.
We have done that for nineteen years knowing it washes off. That is not stupidity, it is the point.
I can find any doorway under this village by feel, in the dark, with my eyes shut. I have had to.
The brick under the water is a red that nobody fires any more. You can pick out the old walls by colour alone.
There is a boat out here named for a woman who drowned and we all say the name perfectly normally.
We float over houses and argue about a carved city that none of us will ever stand in front of.
Somebody chalked a marker line on the mill. Meaning: it stops there. It stops nowhere.
I did not rub it off. You do not rub off the thing that got somebody through the winter.
The wall-walkers stop here for salt and not one of them can swim. Not one, in twenty years.
They walk a wall looking for a hole. We bail a house. Everybody has picked something.
The ring of arches held water in deliberately. We hold water out deliberately. Somebody should note that down.
The uplanders say build like the mountain terraces. You cannot terrace open water. I have explained this.
Everyone out here agrees the tomb is the most beautiful thing there is. Nobody out here has seen it.
The markers stand on dry land while we stand on sticks. That comes up in every argument eventually.
Some families go up in the spring and some do not, and the two halves have stopped eating together.
Swimming comes before walking here. That is not a boast about our children.
We bail until we cannot bail. Then we go. Not one season before that, whatever anybody says.
The names of the drowned houses are being cut into a roof beam, so the beam carries them out.
The children have to know these walkways by heart, in the dark, in wind. That is not a chore.
My mother announced in front of everybody that she will not move, so now she cannot take it back.
The good rope goes on the ladder and everything else gets what is left. That is new this year.
Somebody asked outright how long this row has got. The whole room suddenly had jobs to do.
One of these children will be the one who closes this place up. I know which one. She does too.
Three doors in this village still shut properly. I could take you to all three.
The gulls will take anything you set down for one second. Do not test them. I have tested them.
Turning the drying fish is a job for somebody with patience and I have run out of both.
The bell on the post is for weather. It has been rung twice in my life and both times it was right.
The sand gets in whatever anybody does, and we all still shout about it every single day.
A family left a whole set of pots when they went. We just started using them. Nobody discussed it.
The sea rubs the broken glass soft and gives it back. It is the only kind thing it does.
There is a cart with no wheels behind the last house and it has been there since before my son.
Boats tie where the carts used to turn. There is a ring in the wall for each of those.
The road out goes downhill, then into the water, then it stops being a road.
One more family moves from the bottom row to the top each year. Nobody has ever moved back down.
You can tell how long a house has stood empty by how far the weeds have got up its door.
There is a dark line at the same height on every wall here. That is where it gets to now.
This place has been halfway through leaving for as long as anybody has been standing in it.
We are mid-decision. I know how that sounds. We have been mid-decision for four years.
The beach was twice this wide. There are people alive who walked on the half that is gone.
Waiting on the calendar before we move again. That is what we tell people. It is a way of not deciding.
The house on the corner still has curtains up. Nobody has lived in it for eleven years.
There is a boat in the weeds with a family name on it. That family is three villages up now.
I stand in the empty street sometimes. I do not do anything. Then I come back in.
We took the door off my parents' house and it is our table. We eat off their front door daily.
A child's height is scratched up a doorframe in number four, and then it stops, mid-childhood.
Nobody has taken the doll out of that window, and nobody has ever discussed not taking it.
The bakery oven is still standing in the ruin. I claim I can still smell it. I cannot.
My mother will not walk the bottom lane. She goes the long way round and has for years.
A wall-walker came through last month doing the whole length, looking for the break in the great wall.
His feet were in a state and he would not stop properly. They never do stop properly.
The markers are supposed to show where it stops, which would mean somebody knew in advance.
Every roof beam in this village is cut to the mountain terrace angle. Supposedly. Nobody has ever measured.
Pilgrims go to the calendar stone and come back saying it said nothing, and go again the next year.
My brother argues the carved city predates the water and therefore there was a world before this one.
He is right and he is unbearable about it and those are two separate problems.
We tell the children lions drank at the ring of arches. Not one adult here has seen a lion.
The tomb is the only one nobody fights about. I have never worked out what that means.
We are taking the good beams out of the empty houses before the sea gets to them.
That feels like robbing somebody. It is not. They left. The beams are just beams. I still feel it.
The families who went up send word back and the word is always the same. Come up.
I am teaching my son to mend a roof I do not believe we will still be living under.
He has worked that out. We finished the roof anyway, and we finished it properly.
This year's trees went in on the high ground rather than the garden. That was a decision.
Somebody is writing a list of what has been left behind here so it is at least written somewhere.
If anybody moves the bell, that is the village admitting it out loud. So the bell stays exactly where it is.
I have moved once. My mother says once is enough for one life. She is not wrong, she is just early.
Nine terraces, both sides, weeded by hand. Ask me how my afternoon is going.
Everything up here is carried up. Including the water. I want that understood.
The goats are cleverer than people give them credit for and it has become a genuine problem.
The wind takes the washing every single time and everybody is surprised every single time.
That plum only fruits on the leeward side. Everybody here can tell you why, at considerable length.
Sums in the morning and letters after, every day, for every child, no exceptions.
It is colder up here. People say that to me as though I have just arrived.
This village exists because the one below it went under. That is the whole of it.
We write down where the water reached each year. Date, height, who measured it.
From the top field you can see the sea, and it is nearer than the drawing in the hall has it.
Nobody up here builds below the third post. It is a rule, it has a number, and it is enforced.
We came up four generations ago and there are people here who still say it as though we arrived last spring.
The old road climbs up here and stops at nothing, because the something is underwater.
We can see the stilt village from here. They are on sticks and we are on rock.
They think we are cowards and we think they are fools and everybody is perfectly polite about it.
The ledger has every house lost, the year, the family, and what they managed to save.
It does not record that one of them sang while she gutted fish, in a voice like a gull with a grievance.
Nobody was measuring the singing. That is the flaw in ledgers and I do not know how to fix it.
My grandmother carried plum stones up here in her mouth because both hands were already full.
Four stones, two trees. She is under the smaller one, and the smaller one is the one that fruits.
There are keys by our door for houses that have been underwater since before I was born.
One shelf of the ledger is a single year. One shelf, one year. You can see it from the door.
One chair in this room came out of a house that is underwater. It is the only chair nobody ever fights over.
These terraces are an imitation of the mountain ones. That is not an insult, it is just what they are.
We copied a drawing of a drawing. It shows. The water still takes the soil off the third row.
Do not get the record keeper started on the carved city. I am telling you that as a kindness.
Carved, not built, therefore older than the water, therefore there was a before. That is his case.
He is right. He is also why people have started eating standing up in his house.
The markers all stand on high ground, which people take as proof the builders knew what was coming.
The calendar stone is supposed to predict the water. It predicts nothing. I say that indoors only.
Two of every book, then four. The children copy until their hands cramp and I do not apologise for it.
We are writing down the drowned villages before the last person who saw them dies.
There are four such people left. Four. That is the entire reason for the hurry.
The orchard we planted this spring fruits in nine years. Somebody did that sum deliberately.
The seed jars go into the cave where it is cold. Not to eat. To keep. There is a difference.
The lowlanders will come up eventually. We have already decided where to put them.
We have not told them that. Saying it would be an insult and not saying it is also a kind of insult.
Our job is remembering. That is a strange thing to be handed and I have stopped resenting it.
Thin air, thin soup, thin walls. Somebody says it every day and it stays true every day.
Ice on the bucket most mornings. We wash properly on the warm days and the warm days are relative.
Down takes two hours and up takes four and it is the same path both times.
We burn dung because nothing grows tall enough to burn at this height. You get used to it.
The animals come in before dark and dark is remarkably early up here.
There is nothing to farm, so we keep records. That is not a joke, that is the actual economy.
My fingers will not bend properly in the cold any more. So, I have taken up talking.
From up here you can see the whole coast, and it is a different shape from the map in the hall.
You will not hear the level discussed at this height. People came up here specifically to stop discussing it.
If it reaches us it has reached everybody, so at least we will not be the only ones surprised.
The traders tell us which villages went under this year. Short list. Never an empty one.
Nobody redraws the map. Somebody pencils the new edge in over the old edge every few years.
You can read that map like the rings of a tree, if you know what you are looking at.
We came up two lifetimes ago and we are still the new ones. We will be the new ones forever.
The dead go into the rock. You cannot dig a grave in ground like this and people have tried.
There is a niche with a comb, a fishing weight and a milk tooth in it, and nothing to say whose.
Three people, or one person's whole life. Nobody can tell now. I think that is allowed.
My mother came up from a fishing village and has not touched a boat in fifty years.
Somebody hauled a boat up to this height and left it. No water within two days' walk. Nobody explains it.
The oldest names in the record are all from one drowned place, all in the same hand.
We eat out of a bowl from a house nobody alive has been inside. It is a good bowl. It gets used.
My father still ties knots the coast way and has not seen the coast since before I could walk.
High as the mountain terraces. Half as clever. My father's line and he was not wrong.
The pilgrims want salt and nothing else. They trade badly for it and they will not be talked out of it.
They are looking for the break where the sea came through. Generations of them, at it.
There is no break. I say that here, at this table, and nowhere a pilgrim can hear me.
There is a man up here who owns a drawing of the carved city and charges people to look at it.
It is a bad drawing and it is the only one, so he is doing extremely well out of it.
The calendar stone is meant to say when it stops. Every pilgrim reads it differently and leaves certain.
We take in whoever comes up. There is a room kept ready and it is seldom empty for long.
Nobody asks a new arrival what they left behind. That is not manners, that is a rule with teeth.
The record book has run out of pages twice and we made more pages both times.
Somebody in every generation has to be taught the old handwriting, or the earliest pages become decoration.
Everything is copied into two sets and one set goes deep into the cave, in the dry.
We are planting trees at this height for the first time. Nobody knows whether they will take.
The oldest man here wants carrying down to see the sea once. Nobody has said yes.
Nobody has said no either, and he is not getting any lighter, and we all know how this ends.
Same temperature in here all year. Outside does what it likes. In here does not.
The lamp soot has built a black stripe along the roof, thickest at the height of a walking adult.
That stripe is the only honest record of how long people have walked this passage.
Water drips into the stone basin and fills it by morning. Same rate, every night, for longer than anyone.
The basin is worn into the rock. Nobody carved that. That is just the drip, being patient.
The front chamber floor has been swept so long that it now sits dished in the middle.
Nobody goes past the third lamp without telling somebody. That is the only rule down here that matters.
People have lived in here longer than anywhere. Longer than the villages, by a very long way.
We go in by the upper mouth. The lower one has been under for two generations and it is full of fish.
When a village downhill decides it can no longer keep something dry, that something ends up on these shelves.
We moved the seed jars deeper in after a wet winter, on the grounds that deeper is drier.
There is a water mark on the wall from a flood so old that nobody knows which flood it was.
Give it two generations and whatever your family owns will be in here, labelled, in the dark.
The stone does not move. People say that as though it were a comfort. It only means the stone is not what is moving.
The dead lie in the fourth chamber with their feet towards the entrance, every one of them the same way.
The oldest lie deepest, so walking in is walking backwards through everybody who was here.
A comb, a fishing weight and a milk tooth share one niche and nothing labels any of them.
The seed jars are labelled by hand, and partway along the row the handwriting changes.
The first hand stopped. The second hand carried on. That is the whole story and it is written in labels.
In the dry chamber the books stand spine out. The ones about the sea have gone soft at the edges from handling.
Somebody copied a whole book into the margins of another book, having run out of paper.
My mother's name is on a jar down here. She filled it. It is still sealed and it is staying sealed.
Somebody put their hand in ochre and pressed it to that wall, and then a great many somebodies did the same thing.
That is a child keeping up. Whoever they were, they were made to walk it too.
Seven painted shapes, deep in, all in one row. Somebody wanted the whole set recorded in a single place.
The first two shapes are obvious and then the agreement stops dead. It has stopped in the same place for generations.
Somebody drew the arches in charcoal and then ruled a line across them. Ruled, with a straight edge, not sketched.
Under the line somebody wrote a number. Nobody agrees what the number is counting.
Every serious argument in this village ends up down here. I have never decided whether that is the quiet or the echo.
There are cut squares by the entrance, one to a winter, and the last one has nothing after it at all.
Whoever was cutting them stopped and nobody has picked it up. We all walk past it every day.
Two rows of seed jars. The near row we open when we need to. The far row is waxed shut and stays shut.
You can ask who the back set is for. I will tell you, and then you will wish you had not asked.
Somebody built a shelf down here this year. Planed, pegged, book height, and there is nothing on it.
Somebody measured a future and made furniture for it. I find that either the best or the worst thing here.
The copying happens in the dry chamber. Everything gets written out twice and the second one goes further in.
The children are taught the way out in the dark, by hand, by count of turns. That is a lesson now.
